name: Sinitic (Chinese) Languages

formality.description: Sinitic languages express formality through vocabulary choice, discourse style, and specific honorific/humble forms rather than pronominal T-V systems. Mandarin nǐ/nín (你/您) is a T-V distinction, but most other Sinitic varieties rely primarily on lexical register (formal vs. colloquial word choice, classical vs. vernacular vocabulary). Written Chinese formal register draws heavily on Classical Chinese (文言文) vocabulary.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Sinitic languages have no grammatical gender. In spoken Mandarin, the third-person pronoun tā is gender-neutral. Written Mandarin introduced gendered characters in the 20th century (他 masculine, 她 feminine, 它 non-human), but these are orthographic conventions, not grammatical gender — they are pronounced identically. Other Sinitic varieties generally do not have even this orthographic distinction.

linguisticChallenges.classifierSelection: Every noun requires a specific classifier (量词/measure word) when counted or used with demonstratives. Mandarin has 100+ classifiers; Cantonese has a similarly large set. Using the wrong classifier (e.g., *一个马 instead of 一匹马) is a clear non-native error. The general classifier 个/個 is overused by MT and signals poor quality.
linguisticChallenges.characterVariants: Written Chinese uses two standard character sets: Simplified Chinese (简体字, mainland China/Singapore) and Traditional Chinese (繁體字, Taiwan/Hong Kong/Macau). These are NOT interchangeable — using the wrong variant for the target region is unacceptable. Beyond Simplified/Traditional, there are variant characters (異體字) and region-specific preferences.
linguisticChallenges.topicProminence: Sinitic languages are fundamentally topic-prominent — the topic of a sentence is fronted and may have no grammatical role in the comment. English SVO translations must restructure topic-comment sentences, not just reorder words.
linguisticChallenges.proDrop: Subject and object pronouns are routinely dropped when recoverable from context. Over-generating pronouns (a common MT error from English-trained models) sounds extremely unnatural in Chinese.
linguisticChallenges.tonalDiacriticsInRomanization: When romanized output is needed (Pinyin for Mandarin, Jyutping for Cantonese), tone marks are essential for disambiguation. Omitting tone marks creates massive ambiguity — Mandarin has ~400 unique syllables but ~1,300+ with tone distinctions.
linguisticChallenges.measureWords: Beyond classifiers, Chinese uses specific measure words for uncountable quantities that differ from English conventions. Quantities that are countable in English may require measure words in Chinese, and vice versa.
linguisticChallenges.analyticGrammar: Sinitic languages are analytic/isolating — no inflection, no conjugation, no declension. Tense, aspect, and mood are expressed through particles (了, 着, 过, 会, 要) and adverbs, not verb forms. This means translation from inflected languages requires explicit particle insertion.

notes: Genus card for Sinitic (Chinese) languages (Mandarin, Cantonese/Yue, Wu/Shanghainese, Min, Hakka, Gan, Xiang, etc.). Script is 'Hani' (Han/CJK characters) — all varieties use Chinese characters as primary script. The macrolanguage-zho.json card provides specific properties for the Chinese macrolanguage grouping.
